Daily deep-dive · Day 10

Count-Min Sketch

Track how often every item appears in an endless stream using a tiny fixed grid — trading a little over-counting for memory that never grows with the data.

01The problem, in plain words

You want the frequency of items in a massive stream: how many times each URL was requested, each word appeared, each IP hit your edge. The exact way is a hash map from item to counter — but that map grows with the number of distinct items, and at web scale (billions of distinct URLs) it no longer fits in memory. Worse, the items you usually care about are the heavy hitters — the tiny handful that appear a lot — yet the map pays full price to also remember the billions of one-off items you'll never ask about.

The Count-Min Sketch answers "how many times have I seen x?" from a fixed, tiny table — a few kilobytes, whatever the stream's size — by accepting one honest compromise: its answer is never too low, but can sometimes be a little too high.

Analogy: a wall of tally sheets, each labelled by a different rule — "by first letter," "by word length," "by vowel count." Every time a word walks past, you add a tally to the one bucket it lands in on each sheet. To look a word up later, you read its bucket on every sheet and take the smallest tally. Buckets get shared — "cat" and "car" might collide on the length sheet — so a count can be inflated by a stranger, but the smallest reading is the one contaminated by the fewest strangers.

02The core insight

the whole idea Hash each item to one cell in several independent rows and bump them all. Collisions can only add to a count, never subtract — so the minimum across the rows is the reading least corrupted by collisions.

It's the mirror image of a Bloom filter (Day 2). A Bloom filter uses k hash functions over a bit array to answer membership with no false negatives; a Count-Min Sketch uses d hash functions over a grid of counters to answer frequency with no under-counts. Same trick — many independent hashes, one-sided error — pointed at "how many" instead of "is it here."

03The structure — a grid of counters

The sketch is a 2-D array of counters: d rows (one per hash function) and w columns (buckets per row). Each row has its own hash that maps any item to one of its w columns. All counters start at zero.

Update (add x): for each row i, compute hi(x) to pick a column, and increment that one counter. d counters touched, one per row.
Query (count of x): read the same d counters — hi(x) in each row — and return the minimum of them.
Every counter a query reads was incremented at least once for each real occurrence of x, so no reading can be too low. Other items sharing a cell only push it up.
Taking the min picks the cell where the fewest other items happened to collide with x — the cleanest of the d estimates.

04Why the minimum, and why it's one-sided

Every occurrence of x increments all d of its cells, so each cell holds at least x's true count. The only thing that can make a cell larger is some other item hashing to the same column — a collision that adds its counts on top. So each cell reads true(x) + noise, where noise ≥ 0. Different rows use independent hashes, so x collides with different neighbours in each. Taking the minimum keeps the row where x got the luckiest — the fewest, smallest strangers landing on it.

This is why the error is strictly one-sided: the estimate is never below the truth, only possibly above it. "Never undercounts" is the guarantee you build on.

05The accuracy dial — width and depth

The grid's two dimensions tune two different things. Width w (columns) controls how much over-count you risk: more columns spread items out, so collisions are rarer and lighter. Depth d (rows) controls how often you exceed that error: more independent rows means more chances for one clean cell, so the odds of a bad estimate shrink.

The classic bounds make this exact: pick an error factor ε and a failure probability δ, then set w = ⌈e/ε⌉ and d = ⌈ln(1/δ)⌉. The estimate overshoots the true count by at most ε·N (where N is the total number of items counted) with probability at least 1 − δ. Total memory is just w × d counters — set once, and it never grows as the stream runs.

KnobBigger meansCosts
Width wSmaller over-count per estimate (tighter ε)Columns — linear memory
Depth dLower chance of a bad estimate (smaller δ)Rows — more hashing per op

06The superpowers — heavy hitters and merging

Finding heavy hitters. Pair the sketch with a small list of "candidate top items." For each incoming item, update the sketch, query its estimated count, and if it clears a threshold, keep it in the candidate list. Because counts are never under-reported, a truly frequent item can't slip past the threshold undetected — you get the trending searches, hottest URLs, or top talkers without a per-item counter.

Mergeability. Two sketches built with the same dimensions and hashes merge by adding them cell-by-cell — the result is exactly the sketch of the combined stream. So, like HyperLogLog (Day 9), each server keeps a local sketch and you sum them for a fleet-wide view, shipping a few kilobytes instead of raw logs.

07Key terminology

Frequency estimation
Approximating how many times each item occurred — the question CMS answers. Why it matters: it's a different question from membership (Bloom) or cardinality (HyperLogLog) — "how often," not "is it here" or "how many distinct."
Width (w)
The number of columns per row; buckets each hash spreads items across. Why it matters: it sets the size of the over-count error ε — wider grid, rarer and lighter collisions.
Depth (d)
The number of rows, one independent hash function each. Why it matters: it sets the failure probability δ — more rows, better odds that some cell is collision-clean.
One-sided error
Estimates can be too high but never too low, because collisions only add. Why it matters: "never undercounts" is a hard guarantee you can design around; the noise only ever pads the answer.
Heavy hitters
The few items whose frequency exceeds a threshold — the ones usually worth finding. Why it matters: they're the whole point of frequency counting, and the no-undercount property is what makes catching them reliable.
Linear mergeability
Same-shape sketches combine by element-wise addition into the union's sketch. Why it matters: it makes CMS distributed-friendly — sum tiny per-node sketches instead of shuffling raw data.

08Where it's used

Networking / DDoSPer-flow packet counts on routers to spot heavy talkers and volumetric attacks in fixed memory.
Databases & cachesQuery-frequency and key-popularity estimates to guide caching and admission (e.g. the TinyLFU policy behind Caffeine).

09Common confusions

It over-counts, never under-counts. The estimate is an upper bound on the true frequency — treat an answer as "at most this often," exact only when it happens to be collision-free.
Rare items are the least reliable. A one-off item can read much higher than 1 if it shares cells with heavy hitters; CMS is trustworthy for the frequent items, noisy for the tail.
It's frequency, not membership or cardinality. It won't tell you if x was ever seen (that's Bloom) or how many distinct items there were (that's HyperLogLog) — only an estimate of how often each was seen.
You can't list the items. Like the other sketches, it stores counters, not keys — you can query a count for an item you name, but you can't enumerate what's inside.
Plain CMS assumes counts only go up. The min trick breaks with deletions (decrements can push a cell below the truth); handling removals needs a variant (the Count-Min-Mean or a conservative-update scheme), not vanilla CMS.

10One-sentence summary

A Count-Min Sketch estimates item frequencies in fixed tiny memory by hashing each item into one counter per row of a small grid, incrementing them on every occurrence and returning the minimum on a query — so collisions can only inflate a count, giving a never-undercount, mergeable frequency counter ideal for finding heavy hitters in a stream.
